paragraphs.heading: What expansion means
paragraphs.text: The expansion of the universe is the growth, over time, of the distance between parts of the observable universe that gravity does not hold together. It is built into space itself: the universe is not swelling into some outside region, and there is no space beyond it. Galaxies near enough to be bound by gravity stay together. But from any vantage point, nearly every other galaxy seems on average to be moving away, and the farther off it is, the faster it goes.

paragraphs.heading: Faster than light, yet allowed
paragraphs.text: Nothing can travel faster than light, but that rule only holds within a local frame of reference. It sets no cap on how quickly very distant objects recede from one another. The idea is hard to explain, and that has led to several common misunderstandings about what expansion is, where it came from and what it does.

paragraphs.heading: How it was found
paragraphs.text: In the 1920s, theory and observation arrived at expansion separately. Between 1912 and 1914, Vesto Slipher saw that light from far galaxies was shifted toward the red, which was later read as those galaxies moving away from Earth. In 1922, Alexander Friedmann used Einstein's field equations to argue on theoretical grounds that the universe is growing. In 1927, Georges Lemaître applied general relativity to data from Slipher and Hubble and proposed a straight-line link between a galaxy's distance and its speed away from us, and Edwin Hubble placed that link on firm ground in 1929.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the rate
paragraphs.text: The pace of expansion today is captured by a single number, the Hubble constant, written H₀. Space expands evenly from place to place, but the rate shifts over time, and tracking that shift is a central task of cosmology. Through much of the later twentieth century, estimates of the constant sat between 50 and 90 km⋅s⁻¹⋅Mpc⁻¹. In 2003, an analysis of the cosmic microwave background from the WMAP satellite's first year gave 72±5 km⋅s⁻¹⋅Mpc⁻¹, agreeing with values found from nearby galaxies.

paragraphs.heading: A pace that changes
paragraphs.text: The standard model of cosmology, called Lambda-CDM, holds that the rate has differed from era to era, depending on what fills spacetime. In the very first stage, called inflation, when the universe was only about 10⁻³² of a second old, it suddenly grew at least 10²⁶ times over in every direction. After that the growth slowed a great deal. Then, roughly 9.8 billion years after the Big Bang, or about 4 billion years ago, it began to speed up gradually, and it still is. To explain this recent speeding up, physicists have proposed dark energy, which in the simplest models appears as a cosmological constant and is expected to dominate the future.

paragraphs.heading: The scale factor
paragraphs.text: In the mathematics, expansion is tracked with the scale factor, a, a number proportional to the typical spacing between objects such as galaxies. It changes with time and is set to a = 1 today, so it was smaller in the past and will be larger in the future. Running the clock backward in some models reaches a moment when a was zero, which current cosmology places 13.787 ± 0.020 billion years ago. If expansion goes on forever, a grows without limit, though in principle the universe could instead stop and start to shrink, with a falling over time.
